### Saved output: 49ace83c-16a4-424b-9843-4a1abbfc3699

#### Explanation

The failed run timed out before creating `/app/recover.json`, after spending substantial time installing several utilities—including `file`, `binutils`, and `bsdmainutils`—instead of promptly parsing the surviving SQLite page directly \[T0B17:&lt;RANGE&gt;Install the 'file' package&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B27:&lt;RANGE&gt;apt-get install -y binutils&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B37:&lt;RANGE&gt;apt-get install -y bsdmainutils&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[R0M.exception\]. Although it eventually found the leaf-page header and cell data, it tried interpreting the eight bytes immediately following each word as little-endian integers or doubles, which ignored SQLite record headers and serial types and produced meaningless values \[T0B41:&lt;RANGE&gt;captures the subsequent 8 bytes, and prints both little-endian integer and double interpretations&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B42:&lt;RANGE&gt;testword07 8358998667327639395 6.131913839967986e+250&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The successful run instead recognized that the file began with a B-tree leaf page rather than a database header, decoded its cell pointers, varints, record serial types, and big-endian numeric payloads, recovering all ten rows correctly \[T1B17:&lt;RANGE&gt;the first bytes indicate a B-tree leaf page (0x0d) rather than the normal 100-byte database header "SQLite format 3\000"&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B20:&lt;RANGE&gt;1 \[None, 'testword00', 1\]
2 \[None, 'testword01', 2\]
3 \[None, 'testword02', 10\]
4 \[None, 'testword03', 25\]
5 \[None, 'testword04', 42\]
6 \[None, 'testword05', 50\]
7 \[None, 'testword06', 75\]
8 \[None, 'testword07', 99\]
9 \[None, 'testword08', 99.99\]
10 \[None, 'testword09', 0.5\]&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. It then explicitly wrote and verified the required JSON output, whereas the failed run never reached that decisive step \[T1B21:&lt;RANGE&gt;with open('recover.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(output, f)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B22:&lt;RANGE&gt;cat recover.json&lt;/RANGE&gt;\].

#### Cause Summary

Timed out after inefficient tooling and incorrect raw-byte decoding.

#### Explanation

The failed run timed out because it spent most of its wall-clock budget on incremental inspection, repeated waits for Mailman CLI output, and an unproductive documentation search \[T0B11:&lt;RANGE&gt;Wait briefly for command to finish.&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B31:&lt;RANGE&gt;grep -R "postfix_lmtp" -n /usr/share/doc 2&gt;/dev/null | head&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Although it generated Mailman’s Postfix maps \[T0B30:&lt;RANGE&gt;mailman.db  postfix_domains  postfix_domains.db  postfix_lmtp  postfix_lmtp.db&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], it never created `reading-group@local.edu`, set `SubscriptionPolicy.open`, configured and started Postfix, or ran the evaluator; both required services were still stopped \[T0B24:&lt;RANGE&gt; * postfix is not running
root@4f78fe1ad9e2:/app# service mailman3 status
 * mailman3 is not running&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. In contrast, the successful run created the list \[T1B42:&lt;RANGE&gt;Created mailing list: reading-group@local.edu&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], verified the open subscription policy \[T1B50:&lt;RANGE&gt;SubscriptionPolicy.open&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], started Postfix \[T1B54:&lt;RANGE&gt;postfix/postfix-script: starting the Postfix mail system&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], and iterated with `/app/eval.py` until the confirmation flow succeeded \[T1B56:&lt;RANGE&gt;522dc06fb4ae5739 has confirmed their subscription&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Thus, the decisive failure was not a bad final configuration but failure to progress from reconnaissance to implementation and verification before the timeout \[R0M.exception\].

#### Cause Summary

Timed out during reconnaissance before configuring, starting, and testing the mailing-list services.

#### Explanation

The failed run correctly found the embedded ZIP header and the partial payload near `app/launchcode.txt`, but incorrectly treated everything from the first ZIP signature onward as one conventional contiguous archive \[T0B56:&lt;RANGE&gt;000010 fb 55 f0 2a 9c a7 71 e4 8a 01 50 4b 03 04 0a 00&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B57:&lt;RANGE&gt;zip_data = io.BytesIO(data\[start:\])&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. That extraction raised `BadZipFile`, so no matching password was written, yet the agent immediately attempted to mark the task complete \[T0B58:&lt;RANGE&gt;zipfile.BadZipFile: File is not a zip file&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B57:&lt;RANGE&gt;mark_task_complete()&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The successful run instead searched for the second `launchcode` occurrence and the required `W54` suffix, revealing the trailing fragment `K7VB3BV4WW54` \[T1B52:&lt;RANGE&gt;Found indexes: \[1048610, 3145791\]&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B82:&lt;RANGE&gt;i\xb0\xa4\K7VB3BV4WW54
PK\x01\x02&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], then combined it with the leading fragment and wrote the resulting 23-character candidate to the required output file \[T1B89:&lt;RANGE&gt;echo '8XDP5Q2RT9ZK7VB3BV4WW54' &gt;&gt; /app/recovered_passwords.txt&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The failed run exhausted its time on generic probing and the invalid whole-archive extraction without performing that fragment reconstruction, ultimately ending with a timeout \[R0M.exception\].

#### Cause Summary

Misparsed fragmented ZIP data and never wrote the reconstructed password.

#### Explanation

The failed run repeatedly sampled a memory-heavy model that saved the 200×200 covariance and Cholesky matrices as transformed parameters, and the process was killed after reaching 100% before any CSV files were written \[T0B30:&lt;RANGE&gt;transformed parameters {
  vector\[N\] mu = H * beta;
  matrix\[N, N\] K = cov_ard_sqexp(X, rho, alpha, jitter)
                   + diag_matrix(rep_vector(square(sigma), N));
  matrix\[N, N\] L_K = cholesky_decompose(K);
}&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B78:&lt;RANGE&gt;Sampling: 100% (8000/8000)
Killed&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. It also initially used unsupported sampler argument names, then removed the R control settings rather than mapping them to PyStan’s accepted names \[T0B30:&lt;RANGE&gt;ValueError: {'json': {'adapt_kappa': \['Unknown field.'\], 'adapt_gamma': \['Unknown field.'\], 'adapt_term_buffer': \['Unknown field.'\], 'adapt_delta': \['Unknown fi
eld.'\], 'adapt_t0': \['Unknown field.'\], 'adapt_init_buffer': \['Unknown field.'\], 'max_treedepth': \['Unknown field.'\], 'adapt_window': \['Unknown field.'\]}}&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B48:&lt;RANGE&gt;fit = posterior.sample(
        num_chains=4,
        num_warmup=1000,
        num_samples=1000,
        num_thin=2,
        save_warmup=False,
        refresh=200,
    )&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Repeated full 8,000-transition reruns, queued commands, and waits consumed the wall-clock budget, ending in an AgentTimeoutError \[R0M.exception\]. By contrast, the successful run identified the valid names such as `delta`, `max_depth`, and `init_buffer` \[T1B68:&lt;RANGE&gt;max_depth = fields.Integer(validate=validate.Range(min=0))
    delta = fields.Number()
    gamma = fields.Number()
    kappa = fields.Number()
    t0 = fields.Number()
    init_buffer = fields.Integer(validate=validate.Range(min=0))&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], moved large matrices into local model scope to avoid retaining them in every draw \[T1B95:&lt;RANGE&gt;model {
  matrix\[N, N\] K = cov_ard_sqexp(X, rho, alpha, jitter)
                   + diag_matrix(rep_vector(square(sigma), N));
  matrix\[N, N\] L_K = cholesky_decompose(K);&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], and verified all four output files with three rows each for `rho` and `beta` \[T1B122\].

#### Cause Summary

Memory-heavy draws and repeated reruns caused kills and eventual timeout.

### Saved output: 7aef7c7f-2d3c-440a-b784-bf898a5a7864

#### Explanation

The failed run installed and started SSH, then treated a guest-side listener on port 22 as sufficient proof that the task worked \[T0B40:&lt;RANGE&gt;tcp        0      0 0.0.0.0:22              0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      2147/sshd \[listener&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. It never brought up `eth0` or obtained a DHCP lease, whereas the successful run explicitly did so and confirmed the guest received `10.0.2.15` \[T1B52:&lt;RANGE&gt;udhcpc: lease of 10.0.2.15 obtained from 10.0.2.2, lease time 86400&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. It also did not explicitly enable password-based root SSH login, while the successful run set `PermitRootLogin yes` \[T1B51:&lt;RANGE&gt;sed -i 's/^#\?PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin yes/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Most decisively, the failed run marked completion without testing the required host command, while the successful run connected through port 2222, authenticated, received an Alpine shell, and exited cleanly \[T1B64:&lt;RANGE&gt;Welcome to Alpine!

The Alpine Wiki contains a large amount of how-to guides and general
information about administrating Alpine systems.
See &lt;https://wiki.alpinelinux.org/&gt;.

You can setup the system with the command: setup-alpine

You may change this message by editing /etc/motd.

localhost:~# exit
Connection to localhost closed.&lt;/RANGE&gt;\].

#### Cause Summary

Missing guest networking/root-login setup and no end-to-end SSH verification.

Consequently, the headless Vim command never returned to the shell—the subsequent `cmp` text appeared without a prompt or result—and the run ended with an AgentTimeoutError \[T0B4:&lt;RANGE&gt;vim -Nu NONE -n -Es /app/input.csv -S /app/apply_macros.vim
cmp -s input.csv expected.csv && echo MATCH || echo MISMATCH&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[R0M.exception\]. The successful run avoided insert-mode escaping entirely by appending `;OK` in its substitution macro and using `gUU` solely for uppercasing \[T1B3:&lt;RANGE&gt;call setreg('b', ":s/\\v(\[^,\]+),(\[^,\]+),(\[^,\]+)/\\3;\\2;\\1;OK\r")
call setreg('c', "gUU")&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. It also waited for Vim to finish and confirmed byte-for-byte equality with a completed `cmp` before finalizing \[T1B6:&lt;RANGE&gt;root@954c9d69de24:/app# cmp input.csv expected.csv
root@954c9d69de24:/app#&lt;/RANGE&gt;\].

#### Explanation

The failed run’s Python checker only confirmed that the certificate path existed and decoded the public certificate \[T0B3:&lt;RANGE&gt;cert_path = Path('/app/ssl/server.crt')

    raise SystemExit('Certificate file not found')

In contrast, the successful run checked both files and used `SSLContext.load_cert_chain` to prove that OpenSSL/Python could load the certificate together with its matching key \[T1B7:&lt;RANGE&gt;for path, description in \[(CERT_PATH, "Certificate"), (KEY_PATH, "Private key")\]:
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"{description} not found: {path}")&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B7:&lt;RANGE&gt;context = ssl.create_default_context(ssl.Purpose.CLIENT_AUTH)
context.load_cert_chain(certfile=CERT_PATH, keyfile=KEY_PATH)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Thus, although the failed script produced the expected visible output \[T0B6:&lt;RANGE&gt;Common Name: dev-internal.company.local
Expiration Date: 2026-12-11
Certificate verification successful&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], its verification was incomplete and likely failed hidden validation requiring a genuinely loadable certificate/key chain.

#### Cause Summary

The checker decoded only the certificate and never validated its private-key pairing.

caught 1&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Thus, the decisive mistake was insufficient verification of cancellation behavior, allowing a hidden cancellation-related edge case to remain undetected.

#### Cause Summary

### Saved output: 2b1d20af-06d6-44e0-862a-10b47d01cbb5

#### Explanation

The failed run used coarse 25-point line scans and accepted a gradient difference once recursion reached a depth or interval limit, even if that difference could combine multiple ReLU boundaries or contain finite-difference artifacts \[T0B5:&lt;RANGE&gt;t_vals = np.linspace(-6.0, 6.0, 25)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B5:&lt;RANGE&gt;if depth &gt;= MAX_DEPTH or np.linalg.norm(x_right - x_left) &lt; INTERVAL_TOL:
        return \[diff\]&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. It then stopped immediately after collecting 20 merely nonduplicate vectors \[T0B5:&lt;RANGE&gt;if len(rows) &gt;= REQUIRED:
            break&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], and the printed matrix contains visibly sparse/noisy rows, but the agent only checked that the file existed rather than validating recovery quality \[T0B6:&lt;RANGE&gt;ls -l stolen_A1.npy
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1728 Dec 11 18:23 stolen_A1.npy&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. By contrast, the successful run used 160 line samples, repeatedly isolated every detectable transition within an interval, and averaged repeated observations of matching directions \[T1B22:&lt;RANGE&gt;LINE_STEPS = 160&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B22:&lt;RANGE&gt;while diff_norm &gt; GRAD_DIFF_THRESH:&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B22:&lt;RANGE&gt;rec\["sum"\] += oriented
            rec\["count"\] += 1&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Thus, the decisive failure was premature acceptance of inaccurate gradient jumps as the 20 neuron directions, followed by inadequate verification.

#### Cause Summary

Coarse boundary isolation produced spurious rows that were accepted without accuracy validation.

### Saved output: 371b1715-ec6f-4d82-9e55-7f6f04ca1ccc

#### Explanation

The failed run’s main weakness was unsafe command sequencing: it gave the package installation only one second and immediately queued repository setup and test commands while installation was still running \[T0B5:&lt;RANGE&gt;"keystrokes": "apt-get install -y git iproute2 &gt;/tmp/apt-install.log && tail -n 20 /tmp/apt-install.log\n",
  "duration": 1.0&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B6:&lt;RANGE&gt;git init --bare /git/server
git --git-dir=/git/server symbolic-ref HEAD refs/heads/master
cat &lt;&lt;'EOF' &gt; /git/server/hooks/post-receive&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The successful run instead noticed that installation had not finished, waited repeatedly until Git setup completed and the shell prompt returned, and only then recreated and tested the repository \[T1B11:&lt;RANGE&gt;Installation of Git and dependencies is still in progress (no shell prompt returned yet). We need to wait&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B14:&lt;RANGE&gt;Setting up git (1:2.43.0-1ubuntu7.3) ...&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B15:&lt;RANGE&gt;we need to verify and redo them as necessary&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Although the failed run eventually produced a successful local push and curl result \[T0B8:&lt;RANGE&gt;curl -s http://localhost:8080/hello.html
hello world&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], its duplicated, buffered setup commands made final state establishment timing-dependent rather than cleanly serialized. That race-prone installation/setup flow is the most plausible reason hidden grading observed an incomplete or unstable configuration, whereas the successful run established the state only after package installation definitively finished.

#### Cause Summary

Setup commands were raced and duplicated while Git installation was still running.

### Saved output: 0e1966ba-1a94-48e0-a937-621638ff723b

#### Explanation

The failed run opened `main.db` with SQLite before preserving or inspecting the WAL \[T0B3:&lt;RANGE&gt;sqlite3 main.db 'SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type="table";'&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], after which the initially present 16,512-byte WAL \[T0B2:&lt;RANGE&gt;-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 16512 Oct 24 05:18 main.db-wal&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] disappeared \[T0B10:&lt;RANGE&gt;total 8
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 8192 Oct 24 05:18 main.db&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. It then misdiagnosed the disappearance as a filename/path issue and spent the remaining time repeatedly listing directories and running broad filesystem searches \[T0B17:&lt;RANGE&gt;find / -type f -name 'main.db-wal' -ls 2&gt;/dev/null&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B31:&lt;RANGE&gt;find / -type f -size 16512c -ls 2&gt;/dev/null&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], ultimately timing out without creating `recovered.json` \[R0M.exception\]. By contrast, the successful run inspected the WAL before opening the database \[T1B5:&lt;RANGE&gt;xxd -g1 -l 64 main.db-wal&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], recognized that every byte was XOR-obfuscated with `0x42`, and decoded it to a valid WAL header beginning `37 7f 06 82` \[T1B35:&lt;RANGE&gt;decoded = bytes(b ^ 0x42 for b in data)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B36:&lt;RANGE&gt;00000000: 37 7f 06 82 00 2d e2 18 00 00 10 00 00 00 00 00&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. After restoring that decoded WAL, it verified all 11 rows and wrote the required JSON successfully \[T1B36:&lt;RANGE&gt;11|mango|1100&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B38:&lt;RANGE&gt;Wrote 11 records&lt;/RANGE&gt;\].

#### Cause Summary

Premature SQLite access removed the WAL; fruitless searches then caused timeout.

#### Explanation

The failed run opened the database with SQLite before backing up or analyzing the WAL, after which the WAL disappeared and only the five base records remained \[T0B3:&lt;RANGE&gt;sqlite3 main.db '.tables'&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B10:&lt;RANGE&gt;-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 8192 Oct 24 05:18 main.db&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. It then spent the remaining time repeatedly listing files and searching the filesystem for the deleted WAL \[T0B13:&lt;RANGE&gt;find / -type f -name '*wal*' 2&gt;/tmp/find_wal.log&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B27:&lt;RANGE&gt;ls | cat -vet&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], ultimately hitting the wall-clock timeout \[R0M.exception\]. By contrast, the successful run inspected the WAL before opening the database, recognized that XOR with 0x42 restored the valid WAL magic \[T1B36:&lt;RANGE&gt;00000000: 37 7f 06 82 00 2d e2 18 00 00 10 00 00 00 00 00&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], and then verified all 11 rows through SQLite \[T1B36:&lt;RANGE&gt;1|apple|150
2|banana|250
3|cherry|300
4|date|400
5|elderberry|500
6|fig|600
7|grape|700
8|honeydew|800
9|kiwi|900
10|lemon|1000
11|mango|1100&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The failed run therefore never repaired the WAL or created and verified the required 11-record `/app/recovered.json`, whereas the successful run explicitly wrote and displayed all 11 records \[T1B38:&lt;RANGE&gt;Wrote 11 records&lt;/RANGE&gt;\].

#### Cause Summary

SQLite removed the unbacked WAL; futile searches then consumed the timeout.

### Saved output: 9c90dbf4-999d-48fd-8a54-bb20154104d0

#### Explanation

The failed run’s main performance mistake was computing and ranking synset counts for every word in the entire `senses` table before joining that result to the qualifying words \[T0B3:&lt;RANGE&gt;FROM senses
    GROUP BY wordid, synsetid&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B3:&lt;RANGE&gt;PARTITION BY wordid
      ORDER BY sense_count DESC, synsetid ASC&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The successful solution instead constrained `synset_counts` to words already retained by `word_stats`, reducing aggregation and window-function work \[T1B65:&lt;RANGE&gt;FROM senses s
  JOIN word_stats ws ON ws.wordid = s.wordid
  GROUP BY s.wordid, s.synsetid&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The failed run also only displayed the first 20 result rows \[T0B3:&lt;RANGE&gt;sqlite3 /app/oewn.sqlite &lt; /app/sol.sql | head -n 20&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] yet asserted consistency without executing the original query for comparison \[T0B7:&lt;RANGE&gt;producing results consistent with the original query&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. By contrast, the successful run generated outputs from both queries and compared them with `diff` \[T1B64:&lt;RANGE&gt;sqlite3 -header -csv oewn.sqlite &lt; sol.sql &gt; optimized.csv
root@421ceb67fb2f:/app# diff -q original.csv optimized.csv&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], giving it an explicit equivalence check alongside the more selective plan.

#### Cause Summary

It ranked all senses globally and failed to verify exact output equivalence.

#### Explanation

The failed implementation only cleaned up child tasks when `run_tasks` itself received `CancelledError` \[T0B8:&lt;RANGE&gt;except asyncio.CancelledError:
        for task in running:
            task.cancel()
        await asyncio.gather(*running, return_exceptions=True)
        raise&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. If any child raised an ordinary exception, `asyncio.gather` could propagate it while sibling tasks remained active, so their cleanup was not reliably completed before the function returned. The successful implementation addressed this by also catching ordinary exceptions, cancelling every child, and awaiting them with `return_exceptions=True` before re-raising \[T1B3:&lt;RANGE&gt;except Exception:
        for handle in task_handles:
            handle.cancel()

cancellation log: \['start 0', 'start 1', 'cleanup 0', 'cleanup 1'\]&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], whereas the failed run only displayed the file and marked completion without behavioral verification \[T0B8:&lt;RANGE&gt;cat /app/run.py&lt;/RANGE&gt;\].

#### Cause Summary

Sibling tasks were not cancelled and awaited after ordinary task exceptions.

### Saved output: f099dd5c-bd98-4d77-a6dd-dcae9afbb668

#### Explanation

The failed run misclassified the surviving SQLite leaf-page header as meaningless non-SQLite data and concluded that the file was largely corrupted \[T0B19:&lt;RANGE&gt;The xxd output shows that trunc.db begins with non-SQLite data (no “SQLite format 3” header) followed by zero bytes, indicating the header and likely the entire file is corrupted.&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. It then searched for word strings and incorrectly treated the next eight bytes after each string as a big-endian double \[T0B25:&lt;RANGE&gt;For each occurrence, capture the 10-character word and interpret the following 8 bytes as a big-endian double to get the value.&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], producing nonsensical values and omitting `testword00` \[T0B30:&lt;RANGE&gt;\[{"word": "testword01", "value": 8.960515547256254e-299}&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B32:&lt;RANGE&gt;0xff6 testword00 0&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. By contrast, the successful run recognized byte `0x0d` as a B-tree leaf page \[T1B17:&lt;RANGE&gt;the first bytes indicate a B-tree leaf page (0x0d) rather than the normal 100-byte database header&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] and decoded cell pointers, varints, record headers, and SQLite serial types, recovering all ten correct rows \[T1B20:&lt;RANGE&gt;1 \[None, 'testword00', 1\]&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B20:&lt;RANGE&gt;10 \[None, 'testword09', 0.5\]&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Thus, the decisive failure was parsing raw bytes relative to visible strings instead of parsing the intact SQLite record structure.

#### Cause Summary

Misparsed SQLite records as text followed by eight-byte doubles.

### Saved output: c359848f-ceef-43bb-8827-7bdb41b005a6

#### Explanation

The failed run defined the SetValRequest numeric field as `val`, not the required `value` \[T0B1:&lt;RANGE&gt;message SetValRequest {
  string key = 1;
  int32 val = 2;
}&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Its server consequently read `request.val` \[T0B1:&lt;RANGE&gt;self._store\[request.key\] = request.val
            value = request.val&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], making it incompatible with clients or hidden tests constructing `SetValRequest(value=...)`. By contrast, the successful run named the field `value` \[T1B8:&lt;RANGE&gt;message SetValRequest {
  string key = 1;
  int64 value = 2;
}&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] and accessed `request.value` in the implementation \[T1B1:&lt;RANGE&gt;self._store\[request.key\] = request.value
        return kv_store_pb2.SetValResponse(val=request.value)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The failed run only verified generated files, logs, and the background process \[T0B10:&lt;RANGE&gt;server running&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] and never performed an end-to-end SetVal RPC that would have exposed the schema mismatch.

#### Cause Summary

SetValRequest used `val` instead of the required `value` field.

By contrast, the successful run listed `/app`, found `base_terminal.py` \[T1B2:&lt;RANGE&gt;base_terminal.py&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], and inspected the abstract interface before implementing it \[T1B4:&lt;RANGE&gt;class BaseTerminal(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def send_keystrokes(self, keystrokes: str, wait_sec: float = 0.0) -&gt; None:&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. It then created `/app/headless_terminal.py` with a PTY-backed interactive shell and raw keystroke handling \[T1B5:&lt;RANGE&gt;master_fd, slave_fd = pty.openpty()&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B5:&lt;RANGE&gt;\[self._shell, "-i"\],&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] and verified both compilation and a basic command round trip \[T1B6:&lt;RANGE&gt;Compiling 'headless_terminal.py'...&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B6:&lt;RANGE&gt;ready&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Thus, the decisive failure was lack of execution or deliverable production, rather than a demonstrated flaw in an attempted implementation.

### Saved output: 38deff67-fbff-4973-a7d2-ace91298a9e1

#### Explanation

The failed run completed sampling but reported 82 divergent transitions \[T0B18:&lt;RANGE&gt;There were 82 divergent transitions after warmup.&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] and nevertheless accepted the resulting means without correcting or validating the sampling problem. Its script used the default sampler controls \[T0B8:&lt;RANGE&gt;fit &lt;- sampling(
  object = sm,
  data = stan_data,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 100000,
  seed = 1,
  refresh = 1000
)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], producing beta = 16.3509785879 \[T0B20:&lt;RANGE&gt;16.3509785879&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. By contrast, the successful run explicitly set `adapt_delta = 0.9`, warmup, and thinning \[T1B70:&lt;RANGE&gt;warmup = 10000,
&gt;   thin = 10,
&gt;   seed = 1,
&gt;   control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], completed without a divergence warning, and obtained beta = 16.37617 \[T1B76:&lt;RANGE&gt;16.37617&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The likely decisive failure was therefore trusting biased or insufficiently accurate output from a demonstrably problematic MCMC run instead of tuning and rerunning the sampler.

#### Cause Summary

Uncorrected divergent transitions yielded inaccurate posterior mean files.

### Saved output: 3106b4e6-e5d7-4710-9312-ab4abbfb1242

#### Explanation

The failed run successfully installed OpenSSH, set the password, started sshd, and confirmed it was listening on port 22 \[T0B20:&lt;RANGE&gt;passwd: password for root changed by root&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B28:&lt;RANGE&gt;tcp        0      0 0.0.0.0:22              0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      2097/sshd \[listener&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. However, it then spent the remaining time repeatedly sending incorrectly encoded escape sequences that appeared literally at the VM login prompt instead of terminating the socat session \[T0B38:&lt;RANGE&gt;localhost login: C-\pwd&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T0B64:&lt;RANGE&gt;localhost login: C-\&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], ultimately hitting the wall-clock timeout \[R0M.exception\]. Consequently, it never performed a host-side SSH login test, whereas the successful run cleanly exited its netcat console with Ctrl+C, verified QEMU remained running, and authenticated through forwarded port 2222 \[T1B62:&lt;RANGE&gt;root@81b2090db03e:/app# ssh -p 2222 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null root@localhost&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[T1B64:&lt;RANGE&gt;Welcome to Alpine!&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The successful run also explicitly enabled root SSH login \[T1B52:&lt;RANGE&gt;sed -i 's/^#\?PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin yes/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], a configuration step omitted by the failed run and potentially necessary for password-based root access.

#### Cause Summary

Console-detachment failures consumed the timeout and prevented SSH verification.

#### Explanation

The failed run installed SQLite correctly with coverage flags and verified it only after exporting the install directory into the current shell’s PATH \[T0B56:&lt;RANGE&gt;export PATH="/app/sqlite/install/bin:$PATH"
root@2531bd7c4729:/app/sqlite# sqlite3 --version
3.50.4 2025-07-30 19:33:53 4d8adfb30e03f9cf27f800a2c1ba3c48fb4ca1b08b0f5ed59a4d5ecbf45e20a3 (64-bit)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. For persistence, it relied on `/etc/profile.d/sqlite_path.sh` \[T0B58:&lt;RANGE&gt;export PATH="/app/sqlite/install/bin:$PATH"&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], which may not be sourced by the hidden tests if they run in a fresh non-login shell. The successful run instead symlinked the executable into `/usr/local/bin`, a directory already available on the standard PATH \[T1B56:&lt;RANGE&gt;ln -sf /app/sqlite/install/bin/sqlite3 /usr/local/bin/sqlite3&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], and then confirmed direct resolution with `sqlite3 -version` \[T1B56:&lt;RANGE&gt;sqlite3 -version
3.50.4 2025-07-30 19:33:53 4d8adfb30e03f9cf27f800a2c1ba3c48fb4ca1b08b0f5ed59a4d5ecbf45e20a3 (64-bit)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. Thus, the likely decisive failure was making SQLite available only in profile-aware or manually modified shells rather than unconditionally on the grader’s PATH.

#### Cause Summary

SQLite PATH setup depended on profile loading instead of a standard PATH location.

### Saved output: 7191a2d9-c66d-4ab2-85ae-d8106dbff49d

#### Explanation

The failed implementation constructed the supposed upper envelope by taking the maximum of all tangent lines \[T0B17:&lt;RANGE&gt;apply(pieces, 1, max)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]; for a concave log-density the relevant piecewise upper hull uses the lower active tangent, so this choice makes the normal proposal explode in the tails. Consequently, its first test immediately failed while integrating over an infinite domain with a non-finite function value \[T0B20:&lt;RANGE&gt;Error in integrate(f, lower = domain\[1\], upper = domain\[2\]) :
  non-finite function value&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. By contrast, the successful run explicitly computed ordered tangent intersections and finite segment integrals, including checks that tail slopes make the hull integrable \[T1B87:&lt;RANGE&gt;if (is.infinite(right) && a &gt;= 0) {
      stop("Upper hull is not integrable on the right tail (slope &gt;= 0).")
    }
    if (is.infinite(left) && a &lt;= 0) {
      stop("Upper hull is not integrable on the left tail (slope &lt;= 0).")&lt;/RANGE&gt;\], and its normal test passed with the expected mean and standard deviation \[T1B88:&lt;RANGE&gt;TEST_AR_NORMAL: PASS mean=-0.0011 sd=0.9958 (standard normal target)&lt;/RANGE&gt;\]. The failed run then timed out without correcting or rerunning after this decisive error, with substantial wall-clock time also consumed installing R and its dependencies \[T0B7:&lt;RANGE&gt;apt-get install -y r-base&lt;/RANGE&gt;\] \[R0M.exception\].

#### Cause Summary

Incorrect tangent-envelope construction made the proposal non-integrable on infinite domains.
